question: How can I explain to my young children why we don't celebrate Christmas?
asked: Any practical advice about how I can explain to my children why we do not celebrate Christmas? When we drive around, we see all of the lights and all of the celebrations, and my child is young.
answer:
So this is a psychological question more than a fiqh one. The parent is asking how to explain to, I'm assuming, very young children that we are not celebrating and the other culture is celebrating. So I think that this is a question that is very sensitive to the age of the child, and you should ask those who are more age-appropriate. This is not a fiqh question, but I'll give you some generic advice.

If they're very young, I think one of the best ways is Surah al-Ikhlas, because this is a beautiful, to-the-point surah. We explain that every ummah, every nation, has its rituals, has its festivals. We are Muslims; we have our two Eids.

If they're a little bit older, we can present to them evidences from the Qur'an and from the Sunnah about this issue. Of them is that when the Prophet ﷺ came to Madinah and he found they were celebrating two festivals, he said that every nation has this festival; Allah has given you two festivals better than this one: Eid al-Adha and Eid al-Fitr.

And of course, of the reasons why we do not celebrate other religious festivals is because our Prophet ﷺ said, "Whoever imitates a group of people will be considered to be amongst them." And the imitation that is forbidden, as I have mentioned before, and I will mention in the future as well in a detailed lecture, the forbidden imitation is to imitate the rituals of another civilization and society. This is what is forbidden: to do something that is unique to Buddhism, to Hinduism, to Christianity, to Judaism. Something that is a sign of Buddhism, Christianity, Judaism, Hinduism, we cannot take that and then make it our sign, because that is unique to that faith tradition. So Christmas is clearly something that is a fundamental ritual and a fundamental festival that is associated with a faith tradition. It is not our faith tradition.

And of course, by the way, we can even tell our teenagers a little bit more than this. We can tell them that even early Christians did not celebrate this holiday. In fact, this holiday was invented in the year 320 or so CE, or 350 CE. It was first introduced by Pope Julius I; not even something the disciples did. In fact, many Christian researchers believe that Jesus was born in the spring season, not even in the winter season. Anyway, even if he was born in the winter, it doesn't mean... But the point is, this festival of December 25th does not originate in Christianity. This festival is pre-Christian, and it goes back to a holiday that was found in pagan Rome that is called Saturnalia. And this holiday was to mark the winter solstice, which is basically this season right now.

And this season, of course, is when the time changes. As you know, this is when the short days become the shortest and then they start becoming more and more. And because of this, civilizations across the globe welcomed that this is now essentially the beginning of the new season coming in. So we have the Celts, we have the ancient Nordics, and the ancient pagans of Rome: multiple civilizations celebrated December 25th. Not early Christians; they didn't do this.

However, when the Roman emperor converted to Christianity, they adopted certain pagan festivals. Because as you all know, the Roman civilization used to be pagan up until around 300 or so, when the emperor Constantine made Christianity a state religion and he himself converted to Christianity. Before this point in time, Christians were persecuted. In the same time frame, December 25th, which used to be a pagan festival, miraculously became a Christian festival. It was simply adopted, and it was then made into a Christian festival.

And by the way, a lot of the symbolism and the rituals and the iconography is actually coming from other pagan civilizations. So for example, Santa Claus: they say he is actually Odin of the ancient Nordic gods. He is the god Odin, and he's basically being iterated until he becomes Santa Claus. And other things: the wreath, the symbol of the fir tree, all of this comes from certain pagan symbols. None of it is coming from Jesus and the disciples of Jesus. And even if it did, by the way, come from the disciples of Jesus, we say that's their religion; we have our own faith tradition.

The bottom line: we as Muslims are very clear about this. **Our shari'ah does not allow us to actively participate and celebrate other religious festivals**: any festival that is a symbol and an icon of another civilization, of another faith tradition, in which other gods are worshipped. We are not allowed to participate, and we are not allowed to import those icons. No Muslim should have a fir tree in their house. No Muslim should have special lights and decorations around this time frame. Because every nation has its Eid. Allah is saying every one of you has their own way and their own methodology.

And it's not just us, by the way. Even most of the Orthodox rabbis, most of the Conservative rabbis, prohibit their followers of the Jewish tradition from celebrating the symbols of Christmas, because again, this is something that is not cultural; it is religious.

These prohibitions, of course, are separate when they become cultural; then we can talk about a different issue. And I have given other lectures, maybe one day we'll talk about them: Fourth of July, for example, and other things in which there is no religion. You cannot apply these hadith over there, because there's no religion and there's no 'ibadah being done. And in my humble opinion, those types of celebrations don't come under these hadith at all. What comes under these traditions that are forbidding is when you take a festival that is a holy day, and you then adopt it and you then follow it. This is not something that is allowed. They have their Eid; we have our Eid.

And how you best tell this to your children, it is psychology. I can give you generic advice. I also have four children, and they are at all age levels. I've tried my best, but at the end of the day, how you teach a child is more psychology-related than fiqh. I can give you generic advice, but we cannot adopt these festivals as our own.
